chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Will Marion Cook: erratic genius, the Boston Symphony story
summary: Briggs calls Cook erratic but fine, repeats an unproven rumour about his marriage, and tells how Cook smashed his violin when denied the soloist's chair, which broke his heart because he was Black.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Just usually a few numbers. We played a number like the 'Russian Rag,' and I think all I have is a copy of -- I should have a copy of the contract of -- excuse me a second.
Right.
I should have a copy of a -- arrange musical comedies and things.
Will Marion Cook, yes.
He's the one that started more or less all this. He was a fine person, but I realized he was a little erratic.
He was a little erratic?
Yes, he was.
In what sense?
Not in his work or anything. Well, I'll tell you what I think. They claimed that he married a young woman, his
Briggs
wife, he was forced to marry her because he --
I see.
They claim, but I have no proof of it, you know. Abbie Mitchell, she became one of the very famous prima donnas. She was a prima donna with most of his shows and things.
But they claim, I don't know, if it's just one of those things that you hear, you hear a lot of things, but I have no proof of it.
But he was a -- as far as many -- I hope you don't register that.
No, let's run it.
Yeh, sure, I hope you cut that out.
Well, you can cut it. See, you have to approve of this in any case.
Yes, he was more or less erratic. You got to see -- he suffered, you see. The truth is, he was a first -- not
Briggs 64

soloist, he was one of the soloists with -- violinist with the Boston Symphony Orchestra. He was next to the soloist. And the solo violin died and the Committee, they told him, and he said, "Well, Mr. Cook," when he thought he would replace automatically the soloist. He said, "No, Mr. Cook, you sit in the first chair, but you wouldn't play the solos of a man that played solos."
And he took his fiddle, and he smashed it and walked out.
Smashed his fiddle?
Yes, and walked out.
It was so heartbreaking for Mr. Cook because -- you don't know him, you never seen a picture of him?
I think I probably have.
Well, he was the closest thing to a white, to see him.
He was.
Oh, surely. You had
Briggs
to be a professional to know that he was colored.
I see.
And that broke his heart, he said. Well, let's hope that men will change. They will change, I think.
Well, I hope so.
They'll change in a certain extent.
